title: Sustainability Screened Meeting Rooms › About AVI-SPL Sustainability Screening › Important definitions:
body:
Sustainability Screened Meeting Rooms › About AVI-SPL Sustainability Screening › Important definitions:

- “ **Eligible products**” means the powered hardware products specified within a Reference Design bill of materials (BOM), including displays, collaboration devices, video bars, cameras, schedulers, controllers, audio devices, and other powered electronics. Eligible Products do not include cables, adapters, mounts, brackets, racks, consumables, or other non-powered accessories.
- “ **Science Based Targets**” means validated Near-Term or Net-Zero targets publicly recorded as active in the SBTi database.
- **“Recycled Content**” means manufacturer-disclosed recycled material incorporated into the product or its physical components, including the housing, chassis, and other product components. Recycled content contained solely within packaging does not qualify.
- “ **Energy-Rated Products**” means Eligible Products for which a recognized energy-efficiency certification or rating program exists.
- “ **Recognized energy-efficiency certification or rating**” means ENERGY STAR certification; EU Energy Label Class C or better; or China Energy Label Grade 2 or better.
- “ **Verified Product Carbon Footprint (PCF) data**” means greenhouse gas emissions calculations that have been independently audited or assured by a qualified third party and verified for conformance with recognized standards (such as ISO 14067, the GHG Protocol).

world. It doesn’t mean you can’t do it.

considerations for every country.
This may involve navigating customs,
obtaining local technical certifications
for products, and varying taxes.”

Exploring how software helps minimize your

For companies implementing a larger environmental

central strategy for their sustainability efforts, allowing them
to reduce their carbon footprint and actively contribute
to environmental conservation. These goals can tie into a
company’s broader Environmental, Social, and Governance
(ESG) commitments.

spaces on sustainability
High-impact spaces, like conference rooms, lobbies, auditoriums, and event venues, are essential for businesses to
thrive. Employees collaborate, customers are impressed, and important decisions are made in these spaces. However,
creating these high-impact spaces often requires a significant investment in audio-visual (AV) equipment.
And as technology advances, the demand for more sophisticated and immersive AV experiences grows, too. A modern
conference room might need projectors, sound systems, video conferencing equipment, and interactive displays.
Lobbies that create welcoming, exciting experiences often rely on large projectors and video walls to deliver stunning
visuals. High-impact spaces require more equipment, power consumption, and a larger environmental footprint.
Sustainability goals, however, are becoming increasingly important for businesses. The energy used to power all this AV
equipment can contribute to greenhouse gas emissions. So, while high-impact spaces are crucial, finding ways to make
them more sustainable is essential.

title: IDRC Case Study › Broken Bookings and Frustrated Users
body:
IDRC Case Study › Broken Bookings and Frustrated Users

IDRC’s workplace management system relied on parallel calendars, causing daily headaches.

Users faced inconsistent bookings, incorrect room details, and poor visibility into available spaces. The system caused frequent disruptions and confusion.

Additionally, the platform required admin-level access to remove outdated meetings and lacked floor mapping. As a result, users found it challenging to track what collaboration equipment is in meeting rooms since room information across different tools was inconsistent.

Even minor issues had significant impacts.

“If a meeting room panel went down, users couldn’t check in,” said Paul Levasseur, IDRC’s manager of digital operations and support. “The room would auto-release after 15 minutes, and someone else could book it. We were really eager to return to the Microsoft ecosystem for everything.”

IT turned to Microsoft Places and Teams control panels. However, IDRC wanted a partner to configure and launch this new solution.

**Design**

- Establish a Microsoft Places hierarchy

AVI-SPL mapped six buildings, eight floor plans, and over 70 meeting rooms for locations in Canada, India, Senegal, Kenya, Uruguay, and Jordan.

To ensure IDRC IT experts could seamlessly transition employees to Microsoft Places, AVI-SPL provided remote ‘train-the-trainer’ sessions. Training covered room setup, photo and metadata updates, floor plan changes, and room use analytics.

“We’re not AutoCAD experts,” said Levasseur. “AVI-SPL gave us options. You handled updates for us, offered documentation on Microsoft’s tools, or referred us to mapping vendors. That flexibility helped lower our total cost of ownership, both now and going forward.”

As part of the larger Microsoft Places launch, AVI-SPL installed Microsoft Teams Panels as scheduling devices. Each panel provides room details and supports easy check-in. The AVI-SPL team provided onsite training sessions to help IT validate room panel behavior and check-in experiences.

Over that time, its mission endures: to protect and manage assets and savings, finance projects, protect clients in their day-to-day lives and in their professional activities, ensure secure transactions, and offer the best technological solutions.

AVI-SPL’s part in this undertaking was to equip the new headquarters with solutions that help the client’s people collaborate with one another, as well as their partners and clients.

Over a year’s period, AVI-SPL UK worked with the consultant, macom Group, and the client to provide the AV design and integration into the new Bank Street building, the new UK headquarters. After a series of workshops, utilisation of a proof-of-concept room in one of the existing buildings, and numerous feedback sessions, we worked with the client and understood the kind of capabilities they wanted, we were able to get a sense of what the full experience would feel like and how important the user experience was to the client.

The building has 150 private client meeting rooms and internal meeting spaces. Each room includes a Sharp NEC Display Solutions C-Series display and an HP Slice conferencing system that uses the Skype for Business Platform for collaboration. The rooms also feature a Crestron MD switcher and a Pulse Origin wireless sharing device. With the switcher, attendees can choose which content to send to the display. And the Pulse Origin enables them to share content from their device to the Sharp NEC Display Solutions display.

In divisible spaces across multiple floors, the client’s staff can easily change the configuration of the rooms to suit the style of meetings.

**At a glance.** Organization: Truepoint · Location: Cincinatti, OH · Solution: Professional Services

### Mission: Engage clients with a personalized experience

Wealth management company Truepoint has been growing its team to provide better client service. In the process, it was outgrowing its headquarters, where similar meeting rooms were beset with outdated technology. When leaders found a suitable new home — a blank slate they could tailor to their needs (and still in Cincinnati) — they wanted it to foster a seamless interactive experience between client and advisor.

“Our challenge was to figure out how we want to share ideas internally and how we can best collaborate digitally with our clients,” says Steve Condon, Truepoint president and principal. “That’s something our old space wasn’t set up to do.”

Truepoint specializes in financial advisory services like investment management, estate planning, and tax planning – all of which are enhanced by face-to-face interactions with clients. As this project got underway, the company was already emphasizing a personalized approach to its clients, one that focuses on their life goals and how to achieve them.

That kind of approach would be enhanced with technology solutions that promote a collaborative environment for people gathering in the new headquarters and for those needing to participate from remote locations.

“It was important to us that our office space support daily collaboration and the personal relationships we form with clients,” says Condon.

At the project’s earliest stage, Truepoint completed an internal assessment of the kind of technology it wanted and the likely use cases for its employees and clients. Truepoint Technology Specialist Brad Felix describes the former space as “a jumble of different equipment” spread over two floors. The new home would bring its staff and guests together on one level. When company leadership entrusted AVI-SPL to be the advisor, decision maker, and integrator, they expected guidance about the type of solutions that would realize Truepoint’s goals.

“For us, this whole project has been about reducing the friction between our clients and our advisors when they’re connecting virtually,” says Felix, who adds that AVI-SPL distinguished itself with a vision that aligned with Truepoint’s: Simplify its rooms, create consistent experiences, and make it easy for clients and employees to collaborate in those spaces.

“Our challenge was to shape their collaboration spaces with technology that’s easy to use and reliable,” says AVI-SPL Account Manager Steven Mason. “We had to first determine the UC platform that would be used to make calls and drive collaboration in the conference rooms.”

Truepoint already had experience with Microsoft Teams and Zoom software tools at the desktop level. For the new headquarters, AVI-SPL and Truepoint agreed that Zoom would be the best UC platform to create meeting experiences across a variety of rooms that differ in size and intent: living-room-style areas (for relaxed conversations), traditional conference rooms, and client meeting spaces.

Upon the decision to go with Zoom, there was a lot of excitement about the options for designing Zoom Rooms to meet Truepoint’s needs. Because of its all-in-one capabilities, Poly Trio was selected by both teams as the centerpiece of most spaces, the solution that would be used to launch the Zoom Rooms.

AVI-SPL’s involvement began about a year before construction was complete, and included a collaborative design process that involved various teams from 7-Eleven, representing architecture, real estate, AV and IT.

“Being brought in early allowed us to build those relationships and trust with everybody,” says Austin Figueroa, AVI-SPL VP of sales who works out of the Dallas office.

Figueroa and the team took ideas from different business units and tried to consolidate them into as few and simple systems as possible while abiding by 7-Eleven preferences.

“Any input I gave them, they took that to heart and really worked with me and my team to set up the office like we needed it to function,” says Harvey Dewitt, 7-Eleven market manager.

The joint effort led to rooms where the collaboration process would be easy to engage, whether one is working with peers in the same room or reaching them at remote locations across North America. AVI-SPL designers standardized the install on three different types of rooms (about 100 total): Polycom, Skype for Business/Crestron RL2, and Crestron-controlled huddle rooms.

“Whether you’re in a Polycom room or a Skype room, you just press to join the meeting,” says Elliott. “It’s quick and simple and easy.”

title: Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services › Overview

Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services › Overview

Nov 9 - 2026

A client conversation can influence how a small business funds its next stage of growth. For an individual, a financial discussion can shape how they provide for their family or prepare for retirement. Employees also work with large volumes of company and client information as they make decisions that affect how the organization operates. All of this happens in your collaboration spaces every day.

For CIOs, the challenge is meeting the needs of both clients and employees while giving your IT team a collaboration environment it can protect and support. The experience should feel intuitive for the people in the room and familiar as employees move among spaces and locations. A balanced approach brings those requirements together, so the technology reinforces the professional standards clients expect from the organization.

metadata.page_title: Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services

title: Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services › Start with security
body:
Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services › Start with security

The first consideration is security. Clients and employees need confidence that the conversations and information shared in a collaboration space are protected. In financial services, privacy and regulatory requirements raise that expectation further, so security needs to influence how the room is planned from the beginning.

Room planning gives your IT team an opportunity to make those protections intentional. Teams need to know which platforms and endpoints are approved before deciding what belongs in the space. Access also has to reflect the controls your organization already uses. Making these decisions during design helps IT build security into how the room operates instead of trying to solve for it after deployment.

The room also must support people who attend meetings remotely. A client may join from home while an employee connects from another office, yet both are participating in the same financial conversation. The same privacy and security requirements apply wherever participants connect.

Some complexity is unavoidable when IT is protecting a growing collaboration environment. The challenge is controlling that complexity, so security remains practical to administer as rooms and requirements change. Participants should not have to work through those security layers every time they meet. From their perspective, the room still needs to be straightforward to use.

metadata.page_title: Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services

title: Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services › Make the meeting easy
body:
Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services › Make the meeting easy

A room can meet every security requirement and the experience may still fall short for the people using it. A client walking into a space for the first time should not need a tutorial before the meeting can begin. Employees should not have to call for help with routine tasks. The room should make it easy for people with different levels of technical comfort to start or join a meeting.

A financial advisor may move from discussing a client’s goals to reviewing a plan on screen. An internal team may bring confidential growth strategies into the discussion before deciding how to move forward. In both cases, people need to see and understand the information in front of them without having to think about the room itself. Sharing content should feel like part of the meeting, not a separate task someone has to stop and manage.

title: Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services › Create consistency across spaces
body:
Getting Collaboration Spaces Right in Financial Services › Create consistency across spaces

Different rooms can support different kinds of work and still keep the basic meeting experience familiar. Employees should not have to relearn how to start or run a meeting each time they move to another space. Consistency comes from deciding what should stay familiar even when the space itself is designed for a different purpose.

Standardization gives IT a common foundation for how collaboration spaces operate. During planning, teams can define the platform and core control approach that carries from room to room. They can then decide where a particular use case calls for something different.

This gives IT a clear reference point for technology choices beyond core elements. Additional technology can be selected for the work taking place without changing the elements IT has chosen to standardize.

The same approach also gives IT fewer exceptions to carry forward. When every room is treated as its own project, each new space adds unique configurations and support requirements the technology team must manage.

See how Symphony and HP|Poly Use AI to Power Smart Meetings › How AI Helps AVI-SPL Symphony and HP|Poly Power Intelligent Meetings

Sep 30 - 2025

Today’s post is by guest author Laurie Berg.

AVI-SPL Vice President, Symphony Product Operations

Decades ago, video conferencing and web conferencing (yes, those were the terms used) were not as widespread as they are today. There was continuous presence, which was a 2×2 screen, active speaker mode, lecture mode, and screen sharing. It was helpful to meet with colleagues, partners, and customers when you were not local to each other, but it could be intimidating.

Everything was very manual. Press a button on the remote control to switch views. Move the microphone around to grab the active speaker properly. Nine times out of ten, you left it as is, for fear of breaking something.

A few years ago, we all became accustomed to video collaboration from home, and unified communication and collaboration were taking place around the world. But there were still obstacles. Background noise, such as dogs barking, network struggles, and the simultaneous tasks of listening, reading, and taking notes, all needed to be overcome by the user. Additionally, multi-vendor compatibility had to be addressed.

Today, through the innovation and accessibility of artificial intelligence (AI), we resolved the challenges we had in creating and utilizing conferencing solutions. Collaboration is not only widely used, but it’s easy and more beneficial than we could have imagined.

- **Transcription, translation, and summaries:**  Now we can focus on what is best for us individually. We can listen, read, look, or manage a combination of all three, and rely on post-meeting transcription and summaries to take care of the rest. Let AI be your note-taker.
- **Post-meeting analysis:** We want to make data-driven decisions, but that is easier said than done, as it takes analysis of the data. That is a task many of us do not have the time to conduct. We tend to “go with our gut.” With AI, analysis can be done for us or at least give us a head start. We can discover who engages, monitor typical durations, and more.

All these advancements have changed and continue to change how we collaborate. We have more productive meetings because we aren’t distracted by background noises and fidgeting. We focus on what is best for our individual styles, both leading to better engagement and follow-through.
